newsitem.title: GERMANY: German wage dispute revives bitter 1950s memories.
newsitem.headline: German wage dispute revives bitter 1950s memories.

text.p: FRANKFURT, Oct 27 - German engineering firms, fearing a resurgence of 1950s-style industrial unrest, took a softer line this weekend in a widening dispute over planned cuts in sick pay but they could still face a tough battle.
Union leaders vowed to defend workers' rights to 100 percent sick payments, a cherished privilege won after protracted industrial action 40 years ago, adding they did not fear another long fight.

"We will fight today to defend sick pay just as stubbornly as we did then to establish it," IG Metall union chief Klaus Zwickel told a rally on Saturday attended by 5,000 engineering workers in the city of Kiel on Germany's north coast.
"Nobody can allow illness to be penalised," he said.

The sick pay dispute underlines how far the German labour market has left behind the cosy consensus that cushioned workers in the post-World War Two period, now deteriorating as firms battle against high wage costs and the jobless rate soars.

German engineering firms want to implement a new law allowing a cut in sick payments from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, but none has yet managed to enforce it because of the furious union response.

Hundreds of thousands of workers staged wildcat protests nationwide last week, hitting production at steelworks and car assembly plants, after IG Metall and employers Gesamtmetall failed to find a national agreement on how to cut labour costs.
Calling for fresh negotiations, Gesamtmetall chairman Werner Stumpfe said engineering firms could not afford the production losses a lengthy wage protest would create.

"Every day 500 jobs are lost in the west German metals and electronics industry. With every strike day the risk increases that this number will rise even further. We want to prevent that with a compromise," he told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

At a meeting of employers in Essen on Saturday, Stumpfe said there were alternatives to cutting 20 percent directly off sick pay, such as requiring employees to work an additional 1.4 hours for each day taken off for sickness.
However, he told the Bild am Sonntag: "Cutting costs to secure jobs remains as always an important goal. And excessive sick-pay costs are part of that."

Employment in the metal and engineering sector has fallen since 1991 by around one million jobs to 3.5 million, mainly due to recession and foreign competition, and employers insist high wage costs are an important factor.
Klaus Murmann, president of the BDA employers' federation, told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper that conflict showed that "(companies) can no longer survive labour battles".
Meanwhile the DAG white collar workers' union threatened big protests unless companies dropped the sick pay cut.
IG Metall said it was considering raising its demands for the 1997 wage round following last week's collapse of talks.
The union was initially ready to accept an inflation-linked two percent rise, but only if employers agreed to provide job-security measures, a spokesman said on Sunday.

In an uncharacteristic move, Rainer Eppelmann, head of the trade union wing of the Chancellor Helmut Kohl's CDU party, weighed in on the employers' side to say firms should be allowed to undercut wage contracts if emergency circumstances warranted.

Eppelmann, who has in the past criticised companies for trying to enforce sick pay cuts immediately, told Bild am Sonntag that reductions in holiday or Christmas bonuses ought to be permissible in order to secure jobs.
